subject: psychology
topic: Repeating a claim makes it feel true
angle: While repetition makes false facts feel truer even to people who know they are false, this effect does not appear to apply to social-political opinions.
title: The Mechanics of Repetition

hooks.text: Does hearing a lie enough times make it true?
You think repetition creates belief. It only works on facts.
Your brain is mistaking familiarity for truth.
A screen glows in a dark room. A phrase repeats.
Repetition hijacks your perception of truth.

reveal.headline: Repetition does not make opinions feel true.
reveal.body: While repeated lies feel more factual, this effect does not apply to social-political opinions.

explain.headline: Fluency creates a false sense of truth.
explain.body: Your brain relies on fluency even when you already have knowledge. Repetition makes a statement feel familiar, which your brain interprets as accuracy.

matters.headline: The limits of influence.
matters.body: That may be why you are less likely to be swayed by a repeated political slogan than by a repeated lie about a physical fact.

example.headline: A scroll through your feed.
example.body: You see a fake news story about a chemical. You see it again an hour later. You start to believe it is real.

question.headline: What facts have you accepted simply because you have heard them many times?

stat.label: the largest increase in perceived truthfulness

claims.text: Prior knowledge does not protect against the illusory truth effect, even when the repeated false statement contradicts what a person already knows.
claims.quote: We again find that prior knowledge does not protect against the illusory truth effect. Repeated false statements were given higher truth ratings than novel statements, even when they contradicted participants’ prior knowledge.

claims.text: People sometimes rely on fluency even if they already have knowledge available to them.
claims.quote: Multinomial modeling demonstrated that participants sometimes rely on fluency even if knowledge is also available to them (Experiment 2).

claims.text: The illusory truth effect occurs even when repetitions happen minutes or weeks apart.
claims.quote: Contrary to some theoretical predictions, the illusory truth effect seems to be similar in magnitude for repetitions occurring after minutes or weeks.

claims.text: Repetition does not significantly increase the perceived truthfulness of social-political opinion statements.
claims.quote: A mini meta-analysis combining the present findings with prior work further supported the conclusion that repetition effects for opinion statements are negligible within the tested bounds.

claims.text: Repetition of misinformation makes people more likely to share it because it biases their judgment of accuracy.
claims.quote: the relationship between repetition and sharing was mediated by perceived accuracy. That is, repetition of misinformation biased people's judgment of accuracy and as a result fuelled the spread of misinformation.

claims.text: The largest increase in perceived truth comes from encountering a statement for the second time, with smaller increases for each additional repetition.
claims.quote: The largest increase in perceived truth came from encountering a statement for the second time, and beyond this were incrementally smaller increases in perceived truth for each additional repetition.

verdict: Repetition increases perceived truthfulness for factual information by leveraging fluency, but this effect is limited by the type of content being presented.
caveat: The illusory truth effect may be stronger over shorter timescales and is notably less effective for evaluative or subjective opinions.
caption:
Repetition can trick your brain into believing a lie is a fact.

Research shows that while repetition leverages fluency to make false statements feel truer, this effect is limited. It does not significantly increase the perceived truthfulness of social-political opinions.

Which facts in your life have been repeated until they felt like truth?
